sections.content: Knoxville, Tennessee doesn't always make the headlines the way Nashville or Memphis do. But savvy real estate investors are quietly loading up on deals here — and for good reason. The city offers a rare combination of affordable entry prices, strong rental demand driven by the University of Tennessee, and a local economy that has been growing steadily for years. Whether you're a wholesaler looking for your next assignment, a flipper hunting for undervalued properties, or a landlord building long-term wealth, finding real estate deals in Knoxville TN is more achievable than you might think. If you're just getting started, we recommend reading our full guide to Real Estate Investing for Beginners before diving in.
Knoxville Real Estate Market Overview

Knoxville sits in East Tennessee, anchored by the University of Tennessee and a diverse local economy that includes healthcare, manufacturing, and a booming tourism sector tied to the Great Smoky Mountains. The metro area has a population of roughly 900,000 people, making it Tennessee's third-largest market. Unlike many Sun Belt cities that saw wild price swings during 2020–2022, Knoxville experienced steady appreciation without the dramatic correction that followed. That stability is exactly what long-term investors love.
Average Home Prices in Knoxville

As of early 2025, the median home price in Knoxville sits around $280,000 to $310,000, depending on the neighborhood and property type. That's well below the national median, which gives investors more room to work. Distressed properties — the ones that wholesalers and flippers target — regularly come in between $120,000 and $200,000, leaving substantial room for profit after repairs. Single-family rentals in working-class neighborhoods typically rent for $1,100 to $1,600 per month, and properties near the University of Tennessee can push $1,800 to $2,200 when rented by the room to students.
Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Investors in Knoxville

Not all zip codes are created equal. The key to finding profitable real estate deals in Knoxville TN is knowing which neighborhoods offer the best spread between purchase price, repair costs, and after-repair value (ARV). Here are the areas generating the most investor activity right now. You can explore current deal activity in detail on our Knoxville TN market page.

items: North Knoxville (Fountain City, Inskip): Affordable entry prices in the $130,000–$180,000 range, strong rental demand, and improving infrastructure make this a top target for buy-and-hold investors and flippers alike.
East Knoxville: One of the most active wholesale markets in the city. Median prices are low, distressed inventory is plentiful, and proximity to downtown is driving gradual gentrification.
South Knoxville: Rapidly appreciating thanks to the Urban Wilderness trail system and a wave of younger buyers moving in. Flippers are finding solid margins here as values climb.
Mechanicsville: Close to downtown and UT, this neighborhood offers strong student rental demand. Small multifamily properties are particularly attractive here.

West Knoxville (Bearden, Farragut): Higher price points ($300,000–$500,000+) but strong resale values and demand from owner-occupants. Better suited for experienced flippers with larger capital reserves.
Lonsdale and Beaumont: Deep value plays with the lowest entry prices in the city. Higher risk, but experienced investors who know the market can find exceptional wholesale deals here.

sections.content: Types of Real Estate Deals Available in Knoxville
Wholesale Deals

Wholesaling is very active in Knoxville, especially in East and North Knoxville. The key is finding motivated sellers before their properties hit the MLS. Probate properties, pre-foreclosures, tax-delinquent homes, and absentee owner situations all represent strong wholesale opportunities. Assignment fees typically range from $8,000 to $20,000 per deal, though well-sourced deals in improving neighborhoods can command higher spreads. If you're new to the strategy, start with our guide on Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners to understand the fundamentals before approaching sellers.
Fix and Flip Opportunities

Knoxville is a solid flip market. Labor costs are lower than the national average, and local contractors are generally easier to find than in hotter markets. A typical flip in North or South Knoxville might look like this: purchase at $145,000, invest $45,000 in rehab, and sell at $240,000 for a gross profit of $50,000 before holding costs and fees. That's not a home run, but it's consistent and repeatable — which is exactly what experienced flippers want. Always run your numbers carefully before committing. Use our free ARV Calculator to estimate your after-repair value and our Wholesale Deal Calculator to quickly validate whether a deal makes sense.
Rental Properties and Buy-and-Hold Strategies

Long-term rentals are arguably where Knoxville shines brightest for investors. The city's population of roughly 23,000 UT students creates permanent rental demand in specific pockets. Beyond students, Knoxville's job growth in healthcare (there are multiple major hospital systems here) and manufacturing keeps demand steady year-round. Cash-on-cash returns of 7% to 10% are achievable in the right neighborhoods, which is increasingly rare in today's interest rate environment. Short-term rentals (Airbnb/VRBO) are also popular in properties near downtown and the Smoky Mountains gateway corridor.

Pro Tip: If you're targeting student rentals near UT, look for properties with 3+ bedrooms that you can rent by the room. A 4-bedroom house rented at $600 per room generates $2,400/month — often $600 to $800 more than renting the same house to a single family. Just make sure to verify local ordinances on occupancy limits and rooming house regulations before you close.
Local Market Trends Investors Need to Know

Knoxville has seen roughly 4% to 6% annual appreciation over the past three years — moderate enough to protect against downside risk but strong enough to build equity. Inventory remains tight, which means well-priced retail flips move quickly. Days on market for updated properties in desirable neighborhoods typically run 15 to 30 days. The investor-to-deal ratio is still favorable compared to oversaturated markets like Atlanta or Charlotte, but competition is increasing. Acting quickly on off-market leads and building strong seller relationships is becoming more important every year.

One trend worth watching: institutional buyers have not moved into Knoxville in force the way they have in Nashville. That means individual investors and small operators can still compete effectively without getting outbid by hedge funds. The market rewards local knowledge and hustle over deep pockets — for now.

They're the secondary cities with strong fundamentals, growing populations, and prices that still let you make money on the buy.' — Common wisdom among experienced wholesale investors
How to Find Off-Market Deals in Knoxville

The most profitable real estate deals in Knoxville TN are rarely listed on Zillow or the MLS. Off-market properties — those owned by motivated sellers who haven't publicly listed their homes — offer the best margins for wholesalers and flippers. The most effective sourcing strategies in this market include driving for dollars in North and East Knoxville, sending direct mail to tax-delinquent and absentee owner lists, networking with local probate attorneys, and building relationships with code enforcement officers who know which properties are generating complaints. For a deep dive into sourcing strategies, read our guide on How to Find Off-Market Real Estate Deals — it covers both direct and digital approaches that work in markets just like Knoxville.
Tips for Out-of-State Investors Targeting Knoxville

Knoxville is attracting growing interest from investors based in California, New York, and other high-cost states who want better returns without the price tags. If you're investing remotely, here are the most important things to get right before you commit capital.

items: Build your team first: You need a reliable local agent (ideally one who works with investors), a property manager, and a trusted general contractor before you close your first deal. Don't skip this step.

Understand the sub-market differences: Knoxville's neighborhoods vary dramatically in risk and return profile. A deal that looks great on paper in Lonsdale may have vacancy and tenant quality issues that a West Knoxville property wouldn't. Visit in person at least once before buying.

Use data to validate ARV: Out-of-state investors get burned most often by overestimating after-repair values. Pull comps conservatively and use tools like our free ARV Calculator to stress-test your numbers before making offers.

Account for Tennessee-specific taxes: Tennessee has no state income tax on wages, but it does have a Hall Income Tax consideration for investment returns, and property taxes vary by county. Work with a local CPA familiar with real estate investors.

Analyze every deal rigorously: Don't rely on gut instinct or seller-provided numbers. Learn how to analyze real estate deals like a pro so you can evaluate Knoxville properties confidently from anywhere.

Start with one strategy: Out-of-state investors who try to wholesale, flip, and build a rental portfolio simultaneously almost always struggle. Pick one exit strategy, master it in Knoxville, then expand.

sections.content: Pro Tip: When evaluating Knoxville rentals remotely, use the 1% rule as a quick filter (monthly rent should be at least 1% of purchase price), but don't stop there. In today's interest rate environment, always run a full cash flow analysis including insurance, property taxes, vacancy, and management fees before making an offer. What passes the 1% rule may still cash flow negative after all expenses.

Knoxville is a market that rewards preparation and local knowledge. The investors who do best here are the ones who take time to understand the sub-markets, build reliable local teams, and use data to make decisions rather than emotion. With entry prices still accessible, rental demand strong, and competition lower than in neighboring metros, there's a real window of opportunity right now — but it won't stay open forever.
